Change detection · South Africa

New structures on servitude land, found while they are few

What servitude holders call land invasion shows up from above as cleared plots, new tracks and then structures. We compare dated imagery of your servitudes and known hotspots, flag what is new, have a reviewer confirm each change and send your team a dated, located list after every survey. Land and structures only, never people, and never a judgement on who is entitled to be there.

Used in: Power & utilities · Oil & gas · Rail & roads · Government & public programmes

Request a proposal How change detection works

What it looks like from above

Four stages, and what imagery can see at each

Occupation of servitude and reserve land tends to follow a pattern. Imagery sees some stages clearly and others not at all, and a good survey plan is honest about which.

  1. Ground is cleared

    Vegetation is cut or burnt and plots are marked out. Cleared ground is usually visible in satellite imagery; pegs and string lines are not.

  2. Paths and tracks appear

    New footpaths and vehicle tracks connect the plots to a road. Tracks under tree cover can be missed; a reviewer confirms what the model flags.

  3. The first structures go up

    Small structures appear on some plots. This is the stage where a dated register gives a servitude holder the most options.

  4. The area fills in

    More structures, larger roofs and services follow. From here, the question is a planning and housing question as much as a servitude one.

Why the first survey after it starts matters most

Early knowledge keeps the options open

Once people live in a structure, resolving an unlawful occupation goes through the courts under the Prevention of Illegal Eviction from and Unlawful Occupation of Land Act (PIE Act), with the Constitution’s protection of access to housing (s26) and of property (s25) on either side, and it takes a long time. A 2026 paper by a Rand Water author makes the same point about bulk-water servitudes: the value is in finding encroachment early (FIG Congress 2026).

Early knowledge does not decide anything. It gives the servitude holder time to choose, with the municipality and the community, among options that are much harder later:

  • talking to the people concerned, and to the ward councillor, before anyone has invested in a home;
  • referring the area to the municipality’s human-settlements or land-use department;
  • marking or fencing the servitude, and keeping maintenance access open;
  • a wayleave or an agreement for structures that can stay;
  • planning a diversion of the service, where that is the better outcome.

Our standard

We map land and structures. We do not identify or count people, we do not decide who is entitled to be on the land, and our registers are not eviction evidence. Every decision about a structure rests with its owner, the servitude holder, the municipality and the courts.

How the change is found

A baseline, a schedule and a reviewer

The baseline. We map the structures, cleared ground and tracks along your servitudes or reserve, measured to the line or inside the servitude polygon you supply, and rate each 500 m stretch for encroachment density.

The schedule. Known hotspots are re-surveyed more often than quiet stretches. The interval for each area is agreed with you and set by what the imagery can support: when new dated satellite scenes exist, how often your own teams fly, and, for drone flights we arrange, the permits and authorisations each job requires.

The change. Each re-survey is compared with the one before it. New and removed structures, newly cleared ground and new tracks are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views. Your team receives a notice after each survey saying what changed and where, and the stretches where change is fastest move to the top of the list.

The trend. Over several surveys, the register shows where settlement pressure is growing along the network, which helps your servitude, planning and community teams decide where to spend time.

What you receive

  • A baseline register of structures, cleared ground and tracks
  • A change register after each survey: new, removed and unchanged
  • Before-and-after views of each confirmed change
  • A notice to your team after each survey
  • Outlines of new clusters, and settlement-growth trends by stretch
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers and a PDF report

The imagery

Satellite, your drone flights, and what each can show

Source What it shows well Limits
Dated very-high-resolution satellite scenes Roofs, cleared plots, tracks, change across long servitudes with no flight and no site visit Needs a clear view; how often new scenes exist varies by area; small or shaded structures can be missed
Your own drone orthophotos Much finer detail on the stretches you already fly Only where and when your teams fly; we work from orthophotos or georeferenced stills, not video
Radar satellite comparisons Larger changes such as clearing and earthworks, even under rainy-season cloud Not individual small structures; flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check
Drone checks we arrange Detail on flagged stretches Subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires; within 50 m of people or structures they need specific SACAA approval (drone law)

Every report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as survey imagery.

POPIA

What the register is for, decided before the first survey

Imagery of homes and yards can contain personal information, and a register that ties dated structures to places can become information about identifiable people. POPIA also requires a responsible party to obtain the Information Regulator’s prior authorisation before processing information on unlawful or objectionable conduct on behalf of third parties (s57(1)(b)). Whether a land-invasion register falls within that provision has not been settled in the sources we checked.

So we agree the purpose first. On South African work we scope registers for planning, maintenance and engagement, deliver them only to the contacts you name, and do not package them as evidence about unlawful occupation unless your counsel has confirmed the POPIA position.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Find new structures, cleared ground and tracks between dated surveys
  • Have a reviewer confirm every flagged change
  • Measure each structure to your line or servitude
  • Show where change is fastest, stretch by stretch

What we don’t do

  • Identify, count or follow people or vehicles
  • Survey any area without a break, or promise how soon a change is seen
  • Decide whether a structure is lawful, or who must move
  • Supply eviction evidence

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who built the structures?

No. We map structures, cleared ground and tracks, and the date they first appear in the imagery. We do not identify, count or follow people, and the register carries no names.

Can the register support an eviction application?

We do not package our registers as evidence about unlawful occupation in South Africa unless your counsel has confirmed the POPIA position, including any prior authorisation under section 57. A register records what the imagery showed on a date. Whether and how it is used in any proceeding is a decision for your organisation and its lawyers.

How soon after a structure goes up will we know?

After the next survey that covers it. How often a hotspot is re-surveyed is agreed with you, and depends on when new imagery exists for the area, on cloud and, for drone flights, on permits. We do not promise a detection time.

Can you see pegged-out stands before anything is built?

Pegs and string lines are too small for satellite imagery. Cleared or burnt ground, new paths and the first structures usually are visible, and drone orthophotos show more detail where they are flown.

Our metro already flies drones over hotspots. Can you use that imagery?

Yes, as orthophotos or georeferenced stills. We run the same change detection on them and return the register and layers. We do not work from video footage.

Does cloud or darkness stop the survey?

Optical imagery needs daylight and a clear view. In cloudy months, radar comparisons can show larger changes such as clearing and earthworks, but not individual small structures, so flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check.

Start with the stretches you worry about most.

Send the servitude or reserve file and mark the hotspots you already know. We reply with a baseline plan, a re-survey schedule the imagery can support, and a written proposal.
